extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially Kantian teleology, philosophy of biology, and methodology of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for how to judge natural objects (especially organised beings) with respect to mechanical explanation and teleological (purposive) explanation — i.e., methodological principles for reconciling and using mechanism and final causes in philosophical analysis of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let slip the mechanism of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Always consider the mechanism of nature in products and their explanation; without mechanical principles no insight into the nature of things can be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if one supposes a supreme Architect or predetermined forms, such hypotheses do not further natural knowledge because we cannot know the mode of action of that Being; pursue mechanical explanation as far as possible because it is indispensable to natural science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pass by the teleological principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not exclude the principle of purposes when judging products of nature; teleology is a necessary maxim of Reason for investigating certain natural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleology is a heuristic principle helpful for investigating particular laws and forms (especially organised beings); however Reason must proceed cautiously and not teleologise every productive faculty of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat teleology as reflective, not determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology belongs to the reflective Judgement (a critique of Judgement), not as a determinant principle supplying objective, a priori explanations in natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleology furnishes regulative ideas and a methodology for judging nature according to final causes but does not supply determinate explanatory principles for the origin of natural forms; it has negative and methodological influence on natural science rather than constitutive explanatory force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism and teleology cannot be dogmatically united in one explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the determinant judgement of how a single natural product comes into being, a mechanical derivation and a teleological derivation exclude each other as constitutive explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One method of explanation (mechanical or purposive) excludes the other for constitutive judgments; any objective compatibility must be referred to a ground outside empirical/natural representation (i.e., the supersensible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invoke a supersensible ground for their compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The only possible ground that can render mechanism and teleology compatible is a supersensible (transcendent) principle, though we cannot form a determinate concept of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this ground is transcendent and indeterminate for us, it cannot provide clear explanatory derivations; it only permits the hopeful hypothesis that both principles may objectively cohere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate mechanical explanation to the teleological principle for natural purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging things recognised as natural purposes (organised beings), mechanical grounds must be subordinated to a teleological principle by constitutive judgement of possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although pursue mechanism as far as possible, for organised beings we must assume an original organisation (a causality according to purposes) as the basis from which mechanical laws operate as means toward represented ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain by mechanism as far as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a privilege and duty of natural inquiry to explain products and occurrences in nature by mechanical laws as far as empirical investigation allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing mechanical explanations is rational and meritorious; the limits are set by our human understanding, not by prohibition of the method. Still, where mechanical explanation is demonstrably inadequate, appeal to teleological judgement is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use teleology as a heuristic principle (method of investigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology should be used heuristically to guide investigation of the particular laws of nature and to organise descriptive accounts of natural products according to purposive concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological judgement aids the investigation and description of natural systems (e.g., comparative anatomy), but is not an explanation of their origination or a substitute for mechanical analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish internal purposiveness from external purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal purposiveness pertains to organised beings (their internal possibility is conceived as purpose); external purposiveness is when one natural thing serves another as means to a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only organised beings can be asked 'What is it for?' (internal purposiveness). Non-organised items (earth, air, water) may be purposive externally insofar as they serve organised beings as means; this distinction is essential when assigning teleological predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleologising everything; exercise caution in applying teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason must not attempt to explain teleologically every technic of nature; only where purposiveness is undeniable should teleological principles be invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of teleology makes Reason visionary; excluding teleology entirely makes Reason fantastic. Balance by regarding cases as mechanically possible whenever feasible and invoking teleology only when necessary for reflective judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume an original organisation for biological inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying organised beings, naturalists should assume as basis an original organisation that uses mechanical laws to produce or develop organised forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption allows comparative anatomy and other empirical investigations to search for systematic relations and origins without abandoning teleological judgement; it is a methodological presupposition, not a metaphysical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer epigenesis (generic preformation) over individual preformation and occasionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject Occasionalism (divine immediate production on every occasion) and individual preformation; prefer a system (epigenesis or generic preformation) where nature is self-producing and the generator contains capacities to produce like kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionalism undermines natural inquiry; preformation (individual) demands excessive supernatural intervention. Epigenesis leaves the least to the supernatural and best accords with methodological goals of natural science and teleological judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow mechanical laws to function as means subordinate to purposive causes
rubrics_metrics.description: In teleological judgements the matter, while its form might be judged possible only by design, can nevertheless be subordinated as a means and governed by mechanical laws in service of represented purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits thinking of a universal combination of mechanical with teleological laws in nature's productions without conflating the two principles or replacing one with the other; the compatibility rests on a supersensible ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative anatomy as a methodological tool (the 'archaeologist' of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative anatomy and tracing surviving traces of nature's revolutions are legitimate methods to detect system, analogy of forms, and possible mechanical derivations of purposive structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such empirical inquiry may provide hope for mechanical explanations (e.g., relationships among genera, gradations from simple to complex forms), but it cannot by itself eliminate the need for teleological principles in judging organised beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits: teleological judgements are subjectively valid for us, not objectively decidable about things-in-themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that designedly-working causes must be assumed for the possibility of organised beings is only subjectively valid given human cognitive constitution, not an objective proof about things in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing keeps teleological judgement methodological rather than metaphysical dogma: it guides our thinking and investigation but does not claim ontological demonstration of design in the noumenal substrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish final purposes from mere means in external relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering 'wherefore anything is', either its origin has no reference to design (mechanism) or its presence has a designed ground; very few natural beings claim to be final purposes (ultimate ends) rather than means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traverse nature to see that nothing in nature plausibly qualifies as the final purpose of creation; many things are best understood as means relative to organised beings, which constrains teleological interpretations.
